title: The Signs of Overcollaboration
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece warns that highly collaborative cultures can tip into overcollaboration, where excessive meetings, group chats, and cc'd emails slow decisions and drain productivity rather than improving alignment. It identifies four telltale signs: too many people involved in decisions, communication tools overshadowing actual work, reflexive over-copying on emails, and meetings held just to prepare for other meetings. The article closes by noting that an instinct to over-include people in a decision is itself evidence the organization has a genuine overcollaboration problem.
points: Overcollaboration is presented as a real problem distinct from too little communication.
Four signs are named: too many decision-makers, chat tools eclipsing actual work, reflexive cc'ing, and meetings-about-meetings.
Meetings to prepare for other meetings are flagged as a particularly telling symptom.
The instinct to over-include people in a decision is itself framed as diagnostic evidence.
quotes: In these workplaces, the problem is not that team members communicate too little with each other but that they engage too much.
Overcollaboration is a serious issue and manifests itself in slow and ineffective decision-making and an endless stream of unproductive meetings.
Group chats to coordinate efforts and share knowledge become more important than the work itself.
This collaboration overload reduces productivity and job satisfaction, leading to mental exhaustion and apathy.
Of course, if your instinct is to involve too many people in such a decision, it likely will never see the light of day. That is strong evidence that you truly have an overcollaboration problem.
